title: Area of a circle
intro: In geometry, the area enclosed by a circle of radius r is πr2. Here, the Greek letter π represents the constant ratio of the circumference of any circle to its diameter, approximately equal to 3.14159.

title: Area theorem (conformal mapping)
intro:
In the mathematical theory of conformal mappings, the area theorem
gives an inequality satisfied by
the power series coefficients of certain conformal mappings.
The theorem is called by that name, not because of its implications, but rather because the proof uses
the notion of area.

title: Argument–deduction–proof distinctions
intro: Argument–deduction–proof distinctions originated with logic itself. Naturally, the terminology evolved.

title: Argument principle
intro: In complex analysis, the argument principle (or Cauchy's argument principle) is a theorem relating the difference between the number of zeros and poles of a meromorphic function to a contour integral of the function's logarithmic derivative.

title: Argument technology
intro:
Argument technology is a sub-field of collective intelligence and artificial intelligence that focuses on applying computational techniques to the creation, identification, analysis, navigation, evaluation and visualisation of arguments and debates.
In the 1980s and 1990s, philosophical theories of arguments in general, and argumentation theory in particular, were leveraged to handle key computational challenges, such as modeling non-monotonic and defeasible reasoning and designing robust coordination protocols for multi-agent systems.

title: Arithmetic–geometric mean
intro: In mathematics, the arithmetic–geometric mean (AGM or agM) of two positive real numbers x and y is the mutual limit of a sequence of arithmetic means and a sequence of geometric means. The arithmetic–geometric mean is used in fast algorithms for exponential, trigonometric functions, and other special functions, as well as some mathematical constants, in particular, computing π.

title: Armstrong's axioms
intro: Armstrong's axioms are a set of axioms (or, more precisely, inference rules) used to infer all the functional dependencies on a relational database. They were developed by William W. Armstrong in his 1974 paper.

title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
intro: Arrow's impossibility theorem is a key result in social choice theory, proved by American economist Kenneth Arrow. It shows that no group decision-making procedure based on ordinal utilities (citizens' orderings of different alternatives) can satisfy the requirements of rational choice.
